full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN, with medium confidence.** The behaviour is locally phase-locked patches with low global order and few vortices. It matches the established picture of a locally coupled Kuramoto lattice behaving like the 2D XY model.

**1. Model family.** The rules describe phase oscillators on a lattice with local (neighbour) sinusoidal coupling. `C.KURA(K=0.2)` is a plain Kuramoto lattice. `PHASE_COUPLE(K, p)` looks like the same coupling applied stochastically, so each oscillator updates with probability p per step. I could not verify this reading of the rule grammar. Because of that, I treat the stochastic update as a possible variant, not part of the core model.

**2. Reading the observed features.**
- Local order is very high (p_local_r = 0.973) and global order is low (p_r = 0.119). The frequency spread is near zero and vortex density is very low.
- Together these point to a frequency-locked, locally phase-coherent state. Its coherent domains or smooth phase gradients have different phases, so the global r stays small. Few vortices remain.
- This is the standard outcome of a short-range Kuramoto lattice with identical or weakly disordered frequencies.

**3. What the literature says** (all found in the searches and read in the returned text):
- **Equivalence to the XY model.** The Kuramoto order parameter equals the XY model's absolute global magnetisation. Synchronising from an incoherent start is therefore the same as relaxing the XY model after a quench to T=0 (Levis, Pagonabarraga & Diaz-Guilera, arXiv 1608.02423).
- **No long-range order in 2D.** Short-range 2D XY or Kuramoto systems lack long-range order because of spin-wave fluctuations and topological defects (Mermin–Wagner). This is described in the spin-torque-oscillator Kuramoto paper (Sci. Rep. srep32528, arXiv 1604.01927).
- **Coarsening in the noisy Kuramoto lattice.** With zero intrinsic frequency, the 2D Kuramoto lattice is equivalent to the 2D XY model with non-conserved dynamics. It keeps XY-like coarsening, with correlation length growing as t/log t and vortex density decaying as log t/t. Vortices diffuse, interact and annihilate (Frontiers in Physics 2022, 10.3389/fphy.2022.976515; arXiv 2206.11730).
- **Local coherence without global coherence.** The Kuramoto review (Acebrón et al., "The Kuramoto model: a simple paradigm…") separates global synchronisation from phase locking or partial synchronisation in short-range lattices. It notes global sync is rarely seen except as K and N go to infinity. Another source says the frequencies of many oscillators can sync while the phases stay spread out (MIT 8.334 project note). A local 1D Kuramoto paper likewise notes that frequency synchronisation can occur without phase coherence, with r≈0.
- **Earliest sources for the underlying XY coarsening.** These are cited in the reference list of arXiv 2206.11730: Yurke et al., Phys. Rev. E 47, 1525 (1993); Rojas & Rutenberg, PRE 60, 212 (1999); and Bray's review, Adv. Phys. 51, 481 (2002). I only saw these as reference entries, not their text, so I haven't checked their content.
- **Review.** Bray's "Theory of phase-ordering kinetics" is the review for coarsening. Acebrón et al. is the review for Kuramoto on lattices.

**4. What differs (the possible variant).**
- The probabilistic update (p = 0.03 to 0.1) is random sequential or asynchronous updating. It mostly sets the effective time scale and a little extra noise.
- For the gradient-like, identical-frequency case, this probably doesn't change the phase-ordering class. I did not find a paper that studies p-gated Kuramoto updates specifically.
- That gap could matter if p-gating changes defect dynamics or the fraction of vortices frozen in. I didn't search for it directly, so I don't call it LITERATURE-SILENT.

**5. Confidence.** Medium. The behaviour (local locking, low global r, few vortices) is well covered by the XY and Kuramoto lattice literature. I couldn't confirm the rule semantics, whether the frequencies are identical, or the lattice size. I also didn't read the earliest coarsening papers directly.
